content: Small quantities of infectious substances, including genetically modified organisms (GMOs), classified as Dangerous Goods in Excepted Quantities, can be packaged in primary receptacles. When these substances are packed according to Packing Instructions P620 or P650, no additional requirements from the UN Model Regulations are necessary. An overpack is a container used by a single shipper to consolidate one or more packages into a single handling unit for easier transport and storage. If dry ice is used to maintain the contents' temperature, the overpack may include insulated vessels or flasks to allow carbon dioxide gas to dissipate. When using an overpack, all required markings and labels on the inner packages must also appear on the outermost layer of the overpack unless they are clearly visible through transparent wrapping. Additionally, the word OVERPACK must be displayed in letters at least 12 mm high. Before returning or reusing empty packaging, it must be disinfected or sterilized to eliminate any hazards. Any labels or markings indicating the packaging previously contained infectious substances must be removed or obscured. Some stabilizers may inactivate biological agents, rendering them non-infectious to humans or animals. Proper marking and labeling of packaging materials are essential to provide information about the contents, hazards, and applied packaging standards. All marks and labels must be clearly visible and not obscured by other labels or markings. For example, when dry ice is used as a coolant, the UN number, proper shipping name, and net quantity of the coolant must be indicated, along with the words AS COOLANT. The net quantity of dry ice is critical for determining how long the packaging can maintain a cool temperature and may need replenishment during transit. The net quantity of infectious substances is also important for biosafety and security purposes, as well as for assessing risks in case of spillage or leakage. For Category A infectious substances, the UN packaging symbol and certification marks must be displayed. If an overpack is used, these marks will not appear on the overpack itself. The name and telephone number of a responsible person knowledgeable about the shipment must also be provided. For Category B infectious substances, specific markings and labels are required, including the proper shipping name BIOLOGICAL SUBSTANCE, CATEGORY B in letters at least 6 mm high. Hazard labels, such as those for infectious substances, dry ice, or compressed gases, must meet specific size and design requirements. For example, the infectious substances hazard label must display three crescents on a black circle in the upper half of a diamond, with the words INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE and In case of damage or leakage, immediately notify Public Health Authority in the lower half. The number 6 must appear in the bottom corner. Labels for dry ice or liquid nitrogen must also meet specific size and color requirements. For air transport, packages exceeding passenger aircraft quantity limits must display a Cargo Aircraft Only label. Cryogenic liquid warning labels are required for certain shipments involving liquid nitrogen, except for specialized insulated packaging known as dry shippers. Documentation for shipments of infectious substances must include a Dangerous Goods Transport Document (DGTD) for Category A substances and certain medical or clinical wastes. Category B substances packaged according to Packing Instruction P650 do not require a DGTD. Electronic documentation may be used with carrier pre-approval, but a paper copy must be available upon request. The DGTD must include the shipper's and receiver's information, a description of the dangerous goods, the type and net quantity of goods, handling requirements, and emergency response information. An air waybill is required for all air shipments, including those of infectious substances. It must include the shipper's and receiver's details, carrier information, and a description of the goods. For Category A substances, the statement Dangerous Goods as per associated Shipper's Declaration must be included. For Category B substances, the name and contact information of a responsible person must be provided. Contractual arrangements between the shipper and receiver, such as a Material Transfer Agreement (MTA), are important for ensuring the safe and secure transport of infectious substances. An MTA outlines the terms and conditions of the transfer, including restrictions on use, handling, and disposal, as well as liability, confidentiality, and governing law. In the event of a spill, trained personnel should follow a specific cleanup procedure. This includes wearing protective clothing, covering the spill with absorbent material, applying disinfectant (e.g., 5% bleach solution), and cleaning the area after allowing sufficient contact time.
